cards.title: 1.1 Basic Ideas of Sequence
body: For each of the sequences in task (3) try to find a general formula that describes the given sequence.
**A sequence in mathematics** is a function whose domain is the set of positive integers.
If the domain consists of the first “n” positive integers only, then the sequence is a finite sequence.
Remark: The general formula of a sequence is also known as the nth term formula of the sequence.
For n a natural number n, nfactorial, denoted by n! is the product of the first n natural numbers.

cards.q: What are the first five terms of the sequence given by the explicit formula $$a_n = 4n - 1$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the given formula**
We are given the explicit formula $$a_n = 4n - 1$$ for $$n \ge 1$$.

**Step 2: Calculate the terms systematically**
For $$n = 1$$: $$a_1 = 4(1) - 1 = 3$$
For $$n = 2$$: $$a_2 = 4(2) - 1 = 7$$
For $$n = 3$$: $$a_3 = 4(3) - 1 = 11$$
For $$n = 4$$: $$a_4 = 4(4) - 1 = 15$$
For $$n = 5$$: $$a_5 = 4(5) - 1 = 19$$

**Step 3: Combine the results**
The first five terms are **$$3, 7, 11, 15, 19$$**.

cards.title: 1.2 Arithmetic Progression
body: An **arithmetic progression (AP)** is a sequence in which each term is obtained from the previous one by adding the same number, the **common difference** d = aₙ₊₁ − aₙ.
**General term:** aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d. **Sum of the first n terms:** Sₙ = n/2 · (2a₁ + (n − 1)d) = n/2 · (a₁ + aₙ).
**Arithmetic mean:** if a, b, c are in AP then b = (a + c)/2. Inserting k arithmetic means between a and b gives an AP with k + 2 terms, so d = (b − a)/(k + 1).

**Example (business):** a business makes a profit of 10,000 Nakfa in its first year and the profit grows by 2,500 Nakfa each year. Profit in year 6: a₆ = 10,000 + 5 × 2,500 = 22,500 Nakfa. Total profit in 6 years: S₆ = 6/2 × (10,000 + 22,500) = 97,500 Nakfa.
**Testing for an AP:** compute the differences between consecutive terms; the sequence is an AP only if they are all equal. 3, 7, 11, 15 (d = 4) is an AP; 1, 4, 9, 16 is not.

cards.title: 1.3 Geometric Progression
body: A **geometric progression (GP)** is a sequence where each term is the previous term multiplied by the same non-zero number, the **common ratio** r = aₙ₊₁ / aₙ.
**General term:** aₙ = a₁ rⁿ⁻¹. **Sum of n terms:** Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1 (if r = 1, Sₙ = n a₁).
**Geometric mean:** if a, b, c are in GP then b² = ac, so b = √(ac) for positive a, c.
**Example (growth):** an E. coli cell divides into two every 20 minutes. Starting from 1 cell, after 3 hours there are 9 divisions, so 1 × 2⁹ = 512 cells.
**Example:** in a GP a₂ = 6 and a₅ = 48. Then r³ = 48/6 = 8, so r = 2 and a₁ = 3.

cards.q: In a GP, a₁ = 5 and r = 3. What is a₄?
cards.why: aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹, so a₄ = 5 × 3³ = 5 × 27 = 135. (14 would come from adding 3 each time — that is an AP.)

**Step 2: Find the next term ($$g_5$$)**
Multiply the fourth term by the common ratio:
$$g_5 = g_4 \times r = 1 \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
The next term is **$$\frac{1}{3}$$**.

For two numbers $$a$$ and $$b$$, the Geometric Mean $$x$$ is:

**Step 4: Compute the final square root**
$$x = \sqrt{4} = 2$$
The Geometric Mean is **$$2$$**.

cards.title: 1.4 Harmonic Progression
body: A sequence is a **harmonic progression (HP)** if the reciprocals of its terms form an arithmetic progression. Example: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, … is an HP because 1, 2, 3, 4, … is an AP.

**To find a term of an HP:** take reciprocals, find the term of the AP, then take the reciprocal again. For 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, …: the AP is 2, 5, 8, … with d = 3, so its 10th term is 2 + 9 × 3 = 29 and the 10th term of the HP is 1/29.
**Harmonic mean** of a and b: H = 2ab/(a + b). For positive a, b the means satisfy AM ≥ GM ≥ HM and AM × HM = GM².
There is no simple formula for the sum of an HP.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Which sequence is a harmonic progression?
cards.why: Take reciprocals: 3, 6, 9, 12 is an AP (d = 3), so 1/3, 1/6, 1/9, 1/12 is an HP. 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 has reciprocals 2, 4, 8 — a GP, not an AP.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: What is the harmonic mean of 4 and 12?
cards.why: H = 2ab/(a + b) = 2 × 4 × 12/16 = 96/16 = 6. (8 is the arithmetic mean and √48 the geometric mean; note 8 > √48 > 6.)

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Find the Harmonic Mean between the fractions $$\frac{1}{3}$$ and $$\frac{1}{7}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of Harmonic Progression and Harmonic Mean**
If $$a, m, b$$ form a Harmonic Progression, then $$\frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{m}, \frac{1}{b}$$ are in Arithmetic Progression.
Alternatively, the Harmonic Mean $$m$$ is defined as:
$$m = \frac{2ab}{a+b}$$

**Step 2: Substitute $$a = \frac{1}{3}$$ and $$b = \frac{1}{7}$$**
$$m = \frac{2 \times \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{7}}{\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{7}}$$

**Step 3: Simplify the numerator and denominator**
Numerator: $$2 \times \frac{1}{21} = \frac{2}{21}$$
Denominator: $$\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{7} = \frac{7+3}{21} = \frac{10}{21}$$

**Step 4: Solve for $$m$$**
$$m = \frac{\frac{2}{21}}{\frac{10}{21}} = \frac{2}{10} = \frac{1}{5}$$

**Step 5: Final Result**
The Harmonic Mean is **$$\frac{1}{5}$$**.

Therefore, the quantitative continuous variable is **The yearly amount of rainfall in Asmara**.

cards.title: Sampling methods
body: A **census** studies the whole population; a **sample** studies part of it (cheaper and faster). A sample must be **representative**, otherwise the results are **biased**.

**Simple random sampling:** every member has the same chance (lottery method or random numbers). **Systematic sampling:** choose every k-th member from a list after a random start. **Stratified sampling:** divide the population into groups (strata, e.g. grades) and sample from each group in proportion to its size. **Cluster sampling:** randomly choose whole groups (e.g. some schools) and study everyone in them.
**Example:** a school has 300 Grade 9 and 200 Grade 10 students; a stratified sample of 50 takes 30 from Grade 9 and 20 from Grade 10.

body: **Variable** is the characteristic of interest of an element that can assume different values for the different elements in the population or sample.
Datum: The values that a variable can assume are called data (single measured value (singular of data)) Data or Data Set: collection of numerical / non-numerical values (plural of datum).
Data are facts or figures from which conclusions can be drawn.

cards.title: Frequency distributions
body: Raw data are organised in a **frequency distribution table**: each value or class with its **frequency** (how many times it occurs). **Relative frequency** = frequency ÷ total; **cumulative frequency** = running total.

For **grouped data** choose 5–15 classes of equal width: width ≈ (largest − smallest) ÷ number of classes, rounded up. Each class has lower and upper **limits** (e.g. 20–29), **boundaries** (19.5–29.5) and a **class mark** (midpoint 24.5).
Variables are **qualitative** (categories) or **quantitative**: **discrete** (counted, e.g. number of children) or **continuous** (measured, e.g. height).

cards.title: 2.3 Statistical graphs
body: A **pie chart** is a circle divided into sectors; each sector angle = (frequency ÷ total) × 360°, so the area is proportional to the frequency.
A **bar graph** labels the categories on the horizontal axis and the frequency (or relative frequency) on the vertical axis; bars have equal width and gaps between them.
A **histogram** is used for grouped (continuous) data: the bars stand on the class boundaries and touch each other. A **frequency polygon** joins the midpoints of the tops of the histogram bars.
An **ogive** (cumulative frequency curve) plots cumulative frequency against upper class boundaries; it is used to estimate the median and quartiles.
**Example:** 60 students: 15 walk, 30 take the bus, 15 cycle. Angles: walk 15/60 × 360° = 90°, bus 180°, cycle 90°.

cards.title: Choosing and reading a graph
body: **Which graph?** Categories (favourite subject, type of fuel) → bar graph or pie chart (pie chart when you want to show parts of a whole). Grouped numerical data (heights, marks) → histogram or frequency polygon. Change over time (monthly rainfall) → line graph. Running totals, median and quartiles → ogive.

**Drawing a histogram:** mark the class boundaries on the horizontal axis (e.g. 9.5, 19.5, 29.5, …) and frequency on the vertical axis; draw touching bars whose heights are the frequencies. The tallest bar shows the **modal class**.
**Reading an ogive:** for n = 40 values, the median is read at cumulative frequency 20, the lower quartile at 10 and the upper quartile at 30; interquartile range = Q₃ − Q₁.
**Misleading graphs:** a vertical axis that does not start at 0, or bars of unequal width, can make small differences look large — always read the scale.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If you roll a fair die followed by tossing a coin, what is the probability of rolling a '4' on the first die and getting a 'Head' on the coin?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify the nature of events**
Rolling a die and tossing a coin are independent events because the outcome of one does not affect the outcome of the other.

**Step 2: Calculate individual probabilities**
Probability of rolling a 4 on a fair 6-sided die: $$P(4) = \frac{1}{6}$$
Probability of getting a Head on a fair coin: $$P(\text{Head}) = \frac{1}{2}$$

**Step 3: Apply the multiplication rule for independent events**
$$P(4 \cap \text{Head}) = P(4) \times P(\text{Head})$$
$$P(4 \cap \text{Head}) = \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{12}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The probability of both occurring is **$$\frac{1}{12}$$**.

**Step 2: Identify the repeated letters and their frequencies**
Letter 'S' appears $$3$$ times.
Letter 'T' appears $$3$$ times.
Letter 'I' appears $$2$$ times.
Letter 'A' appears $$1$$ time.
Letter 'C' appears $$1$$ time.

**Step 3: Apply the distinguishable permutations formula**
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{n!}{n_1! \times n_2! \times n_3! \times \dots}$$
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{10!}{3! \times 3! \times 2!}$$
$$\text{Arrangements} = \frac{3628800}{6 \times 6 \times 2} = \frac{3628800}{72} = 50400$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The number of distinguishable arrangements is **$$50400$$**.

**Step 1: State the distance formula**
The distance between two points $$(x_1, y_1)$$ and $$(x_2, y_2)$$ is:
$$d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$$

**Step 2: Substitute the coordinates**

**Step 1: Identify the slopes of both lines**

Since the product of their slopes is exactly $$-1$$, the lines are mathematically perpendicular.

**Yes, because their slopes are negative reciprocals**.

cards.title: 3.3 Circle
body: A **circle** is the set of all points in a plane that are the same distance (the **radius** r) from a fixed point (the **centre**).

If the centre is C(h, k) and P(x, y) is any point on the circle, the distance formula CP = r gives the **standard form**: $$(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$$. With the centre at the origin this is x² + y² = r².
**Example:** centre (2, −1), radius 5: (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 25. Expanding gives the **general form** x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 20 = 0.
**From general to standard form:** complete the square in x and in y. x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 has centre (−D/2, −E/2) and radius √(D²/4 + E²/4 − F) (a real circle only if this is positive).
To plot points, give one variable a value and solve for the other: in (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 25, x = 5 gives (y + 1)² = 16, so y = 3 or y = −5.
**Point and circle:** substitute the point into (x − h)² + (y − k)²: less than r² → inside, equal → on the circle, greater → outside.

cards.q: Find the product matrix $$AB$$ if $$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$ and $$B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Check multiplication compatibility**
Order of $$A$$ is $$2 \times 2$$. Order of $$B$$ is $$2 \times 2$$. Since inner dimensions match, the product is defined and has order $$2 \times 2$$.

**Step 2: Calculate the product entries**
Row 1, Column 1:
$$c_{11} = 1(0) + 2(-1) = 0 - 2 = -2$$

Row 1, Column 2:
$$c_{12} = 1(-1) + 2(2) = -1 + 4 = 3$$

Row 2, Column 1:
$$c_{21} = 2(0) + 1(-1) = 0 - 1 = -1$$

Row 2, Column 2:
$$c_{22} = 2(-1) + 1(2) = -2 + 2 = 0$$

**Step 3: Combine entries into matrix**
$$AB = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The product matrix is **$$\begin{pmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$$**.
